title: TA9-09540
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX is a citizen of Albania. He claims for refugee protection pursuant to Sections 96, 97(1)(a) and 97(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The claimant alleges that he was born in Albania and that, in 1988, accompanied by his family, he went to the United States of America (USA) where his family and he were given their green cards.

In XXXXX 2004, the claimant was with his friends in, Michigan, when his best friend, XXXXX XXXXX, was attacked by an individual with whom he had dispute. That person was also accompanied by his friends when they attacked XXXXX XXXXX. The claimant and his friends went to help XXXXX XXXXX and everyone present got into a fight.

Three days later, the claimant and his friends were confronted by three individuals who were part of the group who had fought with them earlier. They had weapons with which they began shooting at the claimant and his friends. The claimant was shot in his XXXXX XXXXX. His friend, XXXXX, was also shot; he later died because of the bullet wound.

The individuals who had shot XXXXX were criminals from Albania. One of the persons was arrested by the police at the scene but the two were not. Because the claimant made a police report and testified against the three individuals, the families of the individuals declared a blood feud against the claimant.

As a result of the blood feud, the claimant's sister fled from California and his family sold their home. The claimant got addicted to marijuana thereafter. In 2006, he was caught and implicated by the police for being in possession of marijuana for the purpose of trafficking. In XXXXX 2008, the claimant was detained by the immigration authorities and was deported to Albania.

On XXXXX, 2009, upon his arrival in Albania, his father's friend informed him that his neighbours had seen armed people break into his family home in XXXXX. These individuals were waiting to kill him. In XXXXX 2008, his mother's brother in Greece went to seek help from the National Reconciliation Committee to end the blood feud. His efforts did not settle the blood feud and, as a result, the claimant decided to flee to Canada.
The determinative issue in this claim is exclusion under Article 1F(b) of the Convention.

Article 1(F) reads in part as follows: The provisions of this Convention shall not apply to any persons with respect to whom there are serious reasons for considering that: (b) The claimant has committed a serious non-political crime outside the country of refuge prior to his admission to that country as a refugee;

The United Nations Handbook1 defines "serious crime" as a capital crime or a grave punishable act. For the purpose of exclusion under I F(b), this serious crime to have been committed by an applicant "outside the country of refuge prior to his admission to that country as a refugee". The aim of this exclusion clause is to protect the community of the receiving country from the danger of admitting a refugee who has committed serious common crime. Exclusion in 1F(b) of the Refugee Convention is limited to "serious crimes" committed before entry into the state of refuge.2 In this case the state of refuge is Canada.

The Federal Court of Appeal has indicated, without explicitly deciding, that a serious non-political crime should be equated with one in which a maximum sentence of 10 years or more could have been imposed had the crime been committed in Canada. This approach has been characterized as "sensible" and has been followed in the Federal Court Trial Division.3

The claimant in this case is a compulsive criminal. He admitted that he has a criminal record in the USA. Because of the criminal record, he was deported from the USA to Albania and he lost his Permanent Resident status in the USA. Documentary evidence4 is consistent with the claimant's testimony, in that, it confirms that he has a history of criminality in the United States. Moreover, after he lost his status in the USA he entered Canada illegally using his USA Permanent Residence card which was not valid.

The claimant has committed serious non-political crimes prior to entering Canada. The Incident/Prosecution Reports5 from the USA indicate that, on or about XXXXX, 2006, the claimant had in his possession five to six pounds of marijuana. He was caught selling one pound of marijuana to a customer for $1,400.00. On XXXXX, 2006 he was caught again while he sold 200 grams of Marijuana for $1,000.00. On XXXXX, 2006, he was caught for the third time selling 442 grams, 5.4 grams which he said was for his personal use, and one pound of marijuana in a cereal box for $1,400.00. On XXXXX, 2006, for the fourth time, he was caught selling marijuana in a two gallon size zip lock bag for $3,900.00. He indicated that the two gallons of marijuana was of superior quality and, as a result, was worth more money. He was arrested by an undercover police officer and was detained.

His testimony and documentary evidence6 indicates that he was convicted of an aggravated felony related to the illicit trafficking in a controlled substance, a conspiracy or attempt to violate law or regulation of a state in the USA and maintaining a drug house. He indicated that, at the hearing, he was represented by a legal counsel who was retained by his family. He indicated that he pleaded guilty to all the charges against him and, as a result, he was convicted and sentence to two years probation on XXXXX, 2008. He was discharged from the two-year probation under Youth Trainee Status.7

He indicated that, soon after he was convicted, he was taken from his home by the immigration police. He was placed in immigration detention and was tried by the immigration courts. He testified that he was in detention for about eight months after which he was deported to Albania. He testified that he lost his Permanent Resident status in the USA after he was deported from that country.

Each time the claimant committed the aforementioned drug-related crime in Canada he would be tried and punished under Section 5, subsection 4 of the Canadian Criminal Code. Under Sections 5(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Criminal Code, he would have been liable for imprisonment for life. According to the documentary evidence provided by the claimant's counsel,8 section 4(1) indicates that each time a person is in possession of more than 30 grams of marijuana or hashish he is punishable to a maximum of five years of jail term. In this case, the claimant was caught on four occasions while being in possession of marijuana over 30 grams. The same documentary evidence indicates that the punishment for trafficking in marijuana or possession for the purpose of trafficking up to 3 kgs in marijuana is up to five years of jail term. In this case, the claimant was caught trafficking in marijuana on four occasions.

Therefore, based on the evidence adduced, since the claimant was an adult and was caught on four occasions to be in possession of marijuana for the purpose of trafficking, he is cumulatively liable for a jail term of over 10 years and as a result, the panel finds that he has committed serious crimes in the USA prior to entering Canada.

The claimant testified that he pleaded guilty to the charges against him. There is no persuasive documentary evidence before the panel to suggest that the claimant was forced to plead guilty. He was represented by a counsel and hence he had an opportunity to establish his innocence if he felt he was innocent. He did not. There is no documentary evidence before the panel from the USA judiciary to suggest that he was not guilty of the drug-related crimes he was convicted for in the USA.

At the hearing, since the claimant did not provide any documentary evidence to rebut the presumption of a fair and independent judiciary process in the USA, the panel finds that the claimant was convicted and sentenced for the crimes he committed in the USA. Since the USA is a functioning democracy, the panel does not believe that the claimant failed to receive a fair hearing conducted by a fair and independent judicial system in the USA. As a result of the criminal convictions, the claimant lost his Permanent Residence status in the USA and was deported to Albania by the USA authorities.

Based on the evidence adduced, the panel finds that the claimant committed serious, non-political crimes while he was in the USA prior to entering Canada. Since there is no evidence that he committed those crimes for political reasons, the panel finds that the claimant has committed serious non-political crimes outside Canada. The issue as to whether the claimant has completely served his sentence is not determinative as to the legal validity of his exclusion under Article 1F(b) of the United Nations Convention to the status of the refugees, since the Federal Court of Appeal has indicated that exclusion was a possibility even when a sentence was served.9

In Jayasekara,10 in order to rebut the presumption of "seriousness" of the crime the claimant is required to demonstrate with respect to the element of the crime, the mode of prosecution, the penalty prescribed and the facts and the mitigating and aggravated circumstances underlying the conviction, as to why exclusion should not apply to him/her.

In this case, the panel finds that the claimant was an adult when he committed the serious non-political crimes in the USA. In regards to the elements of the crime, documentary evidence11 indicates that the claimant committed the serious non-political crimes in the USA and was convicted by a fair judiciary in USA.

In regards to the mode of prosecution, based on the claimant's testimony, he had the benefit of a legal counsel before he was found guilty of the crimes he committed in the USA. There is no persuasive documentary evidence that suggests that he was innocent and was prosecuted and/or convicted in error. Therefore, the panel finds that the mode of prosecution in the USA was fair and judicious.

In regards to the penalty prescribed, the claimant received sentences in accordance with the USA Criminal Code. His deportation and the loss of his Permanent Resident status in the USA indicate the gravity of the offences he committed. Since there is no persuasive evidence that the claimant's conviction was in any way unfair, the panel does not find that there were mitigating and aggravating circumstance underlying his conviction. Since there is no persuasive evidence to suggest that the claimant's criminal activities in the USA were committed for political purpose, the panel finds that the crimes he committed were "non-political".

Based on the totality of the evidence adduced, the panel finds that the claimant committed serious, non-political crimes in the USA before coming to Canada and individuals like the claimant who have committed serious, non-political crimes outside Canada do not deserve refugee protection in Canada.

Therefore, guided by the case law,12 the panel finds that the claimant is excludable because he falls within the parameters of Article 1F(b) of the Refugee Convention. Accordingly, the Refugee Protection Division excludes XXXXX for refugee protection. (signed) 'S. Alidina' S.
